links.note: 1261 shows the woman's finger worn (தேய்ந்த விரல்) from marking the days since he left (அவர்சென்ற நாளொற்றி); 1269 says that for those pining with the return day in mind (வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்குபவர்க்கு) one day passes like seven. 1269 gives the felt arithmetic behind 1261's tally: the days she counts are each lived as many.

In 776 the warrior takes up his days (தன் நாளை எடுத்து) and files every day without a wound as wasted; in 1261 the wife marks off the days of his absence (நாளொற்றி) until her finger wears down. Both keep a ledger of days, the soldier's reckoned by wounds received and the waiting wife's by absence endured.

In 1262 she tells her friend that if she forgets him today (இன்று மறப்பின்) her beauty will go and her bangles slip; in 1207 she asks what would become of her if she forgot (மறப்பின் எவனாவன்), since even remembering burns. Parimelazhagar frames both as replies to a friend's advice to forget a little, and both refuse it: remembering hurts, but forgetting would be worse.

1262 says forgetting him would cost her her beauty (காரிகை நீத்து); 1250 says that keeping in her heart the man who left (நெஞ்சத்து உடையேமா) will make her lose still more of her loveliness (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்), which Parimelazhagar takes as implying she ought to forget him. On that reading the two speeches assign the loss of beauty to opposite causes; both are the heroine's words in different moods, not the book's settled claim.

615 praises the man who wants the work and not pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as a pillar to his kin; in 1263 the wife describes her husband as gone desiring victory with his own resolve for company (உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாக), which Parimelazhagar glosses as not desiring enjoyment. 1263 shows the same man from inside the house: she stays alive only by desiring his return (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்), the same verb நசைஇ set against his.

In 1206 she lives only by thinking of the days she had with him (உற்றநாள் உள்ள உளேன்); in 1263 she is still alive by longing for his coming (வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்). The two give the same account of what keeps her alive in his absence, one looking back to memory and the other forward to return.

In 1263 she waits for the man who left wanting victory; in 1268, which Parimelazhagar assigns to the man away on the king's service, he wishes the king would engage and win (வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன்) so that he can join his wife for the evening. On that reading the pair gives both ends of one separation: her longing for his return and his impatience for the work to finish.

476 warns that one who has climbed to the tip of a branch (நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார்) and pushes further loses his life; in 1264 her heart, thinking of his return, கோடுகொடு ஏறும், which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read as climbing a tree's branches to look for him (Parimelazhagar reads it as swelling up like a tree putting out branches). On the climbing reading the same image marks reckless overreach in the book on statecraft and eager hope here.

In 1170 her heart goes to where he is, and she wishes her eyes could follow (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்); in 1264 her heart rises thinking of his return (வரவுள்ளி). Both make the heart the part of her that moves toward him while she stays put; on Manakkudavar's reading of 1264 it even climbs to do the seeing her eyes cannot.

In 1187 pallor seizes her the moment she shifts a little in his embrace (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்); in 1265 she says the pallor on her shoulders will leave once she has seen him to her eyes' fill (கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின் நீங்கும்). Together they give pallor's rule in the Book of Love: it comes with the slightest distance and goes only with his presence, which Parimelazhagar underlines by noting that merely hearing of his return will not do.

1283 says her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband (கொண்கனைக் காணாது அமையல கண்) even though he does as he pleases; 1265 prays to see the same கொண்கன் until her eyes are full. Both make the eyes' need to see him the thing that must be satisfied before anything else can mend.

In 1102 the man says that medicine for a disease is normally something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து); in 1266 the woman says that if he comes for one day she will drink him in so that all her sickness is destroyed (பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட). Each lover names the other as both the cause and the only cure.

1101 says all five senses find their objects in her; in 1266 she will 'drink' him (பருகுவன்), which Parimelazhagar explains as drinking that nectar through all five gateways of sense. On his reading 1266 is the woman's version of 1101, with the five-sense enjoyment compressed into a single verb.

811 speaks of people without character who seem to drink you up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as an appearance of excess love; in 1266 she says she will drink him (பருகுவன்) when he comes. The same verb for devouring affection is a suspect show in bad friendship and a sincere vow in the wife's mouth.

1267 asks in advance whether she will sulk, embrace or mix the two when he comes (புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்); 1259 reports what happened: she went meaning to sulk (புலப்பல் எனச்சென்றேன்) and embraced him (புல்லினேன்) on seeing her heart begin to join him. The same verbs recur, and 1259 reads as the answer to 1267's question.

1109 lists sulking, reconciling and uniting (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) as the rewards of those joined in love; 1267 shows the woman, before he has even returned, unable to choose between sulking and embracing and wondering whether to combine them. What 1109 states as a sequence of pleasures, 1267 shows as one impatient wish for all of them at once, which is how Parimelazhagar explains its place in this chapter.

In 1224 evening, when the lover is absent (காதலர் இல்வழி), comes like enemies onto a killing ground; in 1268 the speaker looks forward to an evening feast once the king has won and the couple are together at home (மனைகலந்து மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). The pair shows that evening's cruelty in chapter 123 belongs to separation and not to the hour: the same மாலை is the time set for celebration when they are reunited.

1269 says one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்) for those awaiting the return day; in 1278 she says he left only yesterday (நெருநற்று) and she has been pale for seven days (எழுநாளேம்). Both use seven days to measure how separation distorts time, stretching a day of waiting in 1269 and running ahead of the departure itself in 1278.

1169 complains that the nights now pass long (நெடிய கழியும் இரா), crueller than the man himself; 1269 says a single day goes like seven for those who pine. Both say that separation lengthens time, by night in one and by day in the other.

In 1151 he is told to announce his quick return to those who will still be alive then (வல்வரவு வாழ்வார்க் குரை); 1270 asks what use getting or embracing is once the heart has broken and spilled (உள்ளம் உடைந்துக்கக் கால்). Both say a reunion that arrives too late is worth nothing; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 1270 the man himself now voices the warning that was put to him in 1151, while Manakkudavar gives 1270 to the woman.

709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship (கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know its kinds; in 1271 the man tells her that though she hides it, her eyes have slipped her control and have something to say (உண்கண் உரைக்கல் உறுவது). The minister's skill of reading the eye in the book on statecraft is the lover's skill here, with the same verb உரை for what the eye does.

In 1180 the woman says the town easily learns the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்); in 1271 the man says her eyes go beyond her hold (கையிகந்து) and speak though she conceals (கரப்பினும்). Both hold that the eyes publish what the person tries to keep hidden, said once by the woman of herself and once by the man reading her.

71 asks if there is any bolt to shut love in, since the small tears of the loving announce it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்); 1271 says her eyes tell something despite her concealment. The claim that affection cannot be locked away and that the eyes give it out appears in the book on virtue as a general truth about அன்பு and in the Book of Love as a scene.

1272 says this girl has a great measure of womanly nature (பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது), which Parimelazhagar takes as artlessness beyond the usual; 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading is womanhood added to womanhood (பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்து). The chapter's first observation about her is given its content at the end: her womanliness is her saying it with the eyes and not in words.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart as crystal shows what is next to it (அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்கு); 1273 says something shows through her beauty like the thread in strung gems (மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்), and Parimelazhagar specifies crystal beads. Both use a transparent stone for an inner state visible from outside, as a rule for courtiers in 706 and as a lover's observation in 1273.

1273 compares her unspoken meaning to a thread that shows through the gems (திகழ்தரு); 1274 compares it to the scent inside a closed bud (முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்). Parimelazhagar distinguishes them: the first lies within yet is visible outside, the second is not visible outside at all, so the pair moves from a sign that can be seen to one that can only be inferred.

650 likens those who cannot unfold what they have learned to flowers that bloom in clusters without scent (நாறா மலர்); 1274 likens what is in her budding smile to the scent inside an unopened bud (முகைமொக்குள் நாற்றம்). Scent stands in both for the inner content of a thing: 650 has the outward bloom without it, 1274 has it present before any outward opening.

1227 describes love's sickness as budding in the morning (காலை அரும்பி), swelling through the day and flowering at evening; 1274 places an unspoken meaning inside the bud of her smile (நகைமொக்குள்). Both use the bud for a feeling that is already there and has not yet opened, pain in the one and a hidden intention in the other.

1275 says the stealth with which she acted and withdrew (செய்திறந்த கள்ளம்) holds a medicine for great sorrow; 1279 states what she did (அஃதாண்டவள் செய்தது): she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet. Parimelazhagar ties the two explicitly, taking 1279's அஃது to point back to 1275, so that the silent gesture is the 'stealth' and its meaning, going with him, is the cure.

1091 finds two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (அந்நோய் மருந்து); 1275 finds in her covert behaviour a medicine that ends great sorrow (உறுதுயர் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து). In both the remedy is not anything she says but something to be read in a sign she gives.

1092 values the small look her eyes steal (கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்) at more than half of love; 1275 says her கள்ளம், her stealth, contains a medicine. Theft is the figure for her indirect signalling in both, at first meeting in 1092 and after reunion in 1275.

1152 says his look alone was once sweet, and now union itself carries the pain of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு); 1276 says his greatly comforting, eager union contains her having to endure again and to think on his lack of love (அன்பின்மை சூழ்வது உடைத்து). Both are the woman telling her friend that she reads coming departure in his lovemaking, and both use உடைத்து for what the embrace holds within it.

827 warns not to take an enemy's bowing words at face value, because a bow's bending signals harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்); in 1276 the woman reads his unusually great tenderness (பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல்) as a sign of coming absence. The same inference, that excess of kindness points to its opposite, is advice about false friends in one book and a wife's reading of her husband in the other, though she alleges no enmity.

1157 asks if the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim that the lord of the shore has left her (துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல்); 1277 says the bangles perceived before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted (தணந்தமை நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Same man, same bangles, in both; 1157 has them announce a departure, while 1277 has them detect one that Parimelazhagar says is so far only in his mind.

707 asks if anything is as knowing as the face, which gets there first (தான்முந்துறும்) whether one is pleased or angry; 1277 says her bangles knew before she did (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த). In both the body registers a state ahead of the person, the face ahead of speech in the book on statecraft and her thinning arms ahead of her own understanding here.

In 1185 she points: there goes her lover, and here the pallor is spreading over her body (உவக்காண்… இவக்காண்), the two at the same moment; in 1278 he left yesterday and she has already been pale for seven days (மேனி பசந்து எழுநாளேம்). 1278 pushes 1185's simultaneity further: the pallor now comes before the departure, which Parimelazhagar explains as her having suspected his intention for a week.

1277 says her bangles knew of his parting before she did; 1278 says her body has been pale for seven days though he left only yesterday. The two adjacent speeches make the same point with different signs: her body responds to his intention to leave before the leaving is an acknowledged fact.

1093 reports a wordless act and reads it: she looked, and having looked bowed her head (நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள்), and that (அஃது) was water poured on their bond; 1279 reports that she looked at her bangles, her shoulders and her feet, and that (அஃது) is what she did there. Both verses consist of a sequence of looks followed by அஃது, leaving the meaning to be drawn from the gesture, at courtship in 1093 and at the threat of parting in 1279.

1234 describes separation's effect: the shoulders lose their fullness and old beauty and the bangles slip (பைந்தொடி சோரும்… தோள்); in 1279 she looks at bangles and soft shoulders (தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி) and then at her feet. Read with 1234, her first two glances name what will happen if she is left, and the third, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it, names her alternative of walking with him.

1137 says nothing has greater worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்); 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading (கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு) is womanhood upon womanhood. Both praise as specifically womanly the refusal to declare desire openly, 1137 by what she will not do and 1280 by the silent means she uses instead.

1100 says that when eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல); 1280 praises her for telling her sickness with the eyes (கண்ணினால் சொல்லி). 1280 applies the general statement about lovers' eyes to a hard case, a plea not to be left, and adds a value judgment the earlier verse lacks.

1053 says that even asking has a beauty of its own (இரப்புமோர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when done before those who know their duty and do not withhold; 1280 says her asking (இரவு), done with the eyes, has a womanliness of its own (பெண்மை உடைத்து). The word for begging is the same, and both grant it a grace under conditions, though the chapter on begging means alms and 1280 means a lover's plea.
